prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength are interrogated by the thousand without Doppler or recoil shifts, bringing atomic time keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I have tried in this round to test it rather than defend a count, since three of the five members who now prefer it, myself included, got there after reading each other's openings. The scientific case holds up under the chair's questions. On what is new relative to 2005 and 2012: the frequency comb gave us a way to count optical cycles, and trapped-ion control gave us a single well-isolated quantum absorber with a very small signal. The lattice clock is neither. Its new element is the magic wavelength, where the light shift of the two clock states cancels, so thousands of neutral atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime and are interrogated together. That combines ensemble statistics with single-particle systematic control, a different route to stability, and it is the reason the performance moved by orders of magnitude. I want the citation to say this in words so the distinction is on the page. On credit, I read Katori as the originator of the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium realisation, and Ye as the person who drove accuracy, coherence and the many-body clock to the record level; those are original contributions, not a later repeat of the same experiment. On timing, I still do not think the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second. The discovery is complete and has been reproduced and compared across laboratories, whereas the redefinition is a metrology decision on its own calendar. What I still cannot do from these files is verify the current record uncertainties and the inter-laboratory comparison numbers, and I ask that expert reviewers confirm them before the final ballot.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection has not gone away and I do not claim it is answered for everyone. Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson in particular read some of the novelty as closer to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or as a performance record, and a reasonable committee could decide that three precision-timekeeping prizes in about twenty years is too many. Olsson's rule, that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later and better realisation, is a fair test and it narrows the case for Ye: if his share were only the accuracy campaign, the credit would be weaker than I have said. I think his many-body clock and coherence work, together with the first-class strontium experiment at JILA, is more than a refinement, but this is a judgment and not a certainty. The two-name credit also leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups, as Mehlig points out, and the redefinition has not yet happened, so the application is still ahead of the prize. Finally, B044 is clearly the broader scientific field, with seven members ranking it, and if the committee wants a discovery about nature and not a better instrument, I would understand a vote in that direction. I stay with B018 because B044's credit and interpretation are less settled, not because I think it is weaker science.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B018 but applies the rule that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a second discoverer who did it much better, and asks whether Ye's role is original or a major improvement on Katori's concept, and whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley or Takamoto should be weighed.
responses.response: I accept your rule and think it is the right one for this candidate. Applied honestly it gives Katori the idea and the first strontium clock, and the citation should be built around the lattice concept and its realisation. For Ye I would justify the share on three things beyond a better number: the many-body, spin-polarised lattice clock that showed the ensemble can be used as a coherent resource, the demonstrated coherence times and systematic control that made 1e-18 credible, and the leadership of the JILA strontium programme that other laboratories compared against. If you or Kroll think those do not clear your bar, say so now, because that is the point on which the pair would fail. On Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley, I read them as important members of a field that grew after the concept, and with a three-name ceiling I would not add anyone, but I would like the expert reviewers to say whether any of them has an independent claim on the original demonstrations.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B012 for Young, Halperin and Nelson for its clean attribution and forty years of tests, but concedes the thinnest opening support, the 2016 overlap, first-order melting in some systems, and that he could move if B012 looks like a sequel to 2016.
responses.response: I am not an expert on two-dimensional melting, so I take your account of the theory as given, and I agree that its maturity is not in doubt and that the attribution is clean. My difficulty is the one you raise yourself. When a member's own preferred candidate has one supporter, a 2016 neighbour and an acknowledged non-universality caveat, I would be wary of putting it ahead of a result with five supporters and reproduction in many laboratories. Your suggestion of a two-part prize pairing B012 with B018 is the interesting one, but it costs three names and takes us to five people, which the three-person limit forbids, and a two-name B012 would drop one of the three people whose credit you describe as clean. So I do not see how to carry it. I also note that you place B018 first among your alternatives, so I would ask you whether the magic-wavelength argument above answers your concern that the lattice clock is a second-generation refinement.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B018 as a new measurement capability with Doppler and recoil shifts removed and thousands of atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, but asks whether the 1e-18 milestone belongs to Ye's group or to collaborators, and whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with your physical picture and am glad you separate the lattice from the comb: a comb makes optical clocks countable, and it does not make a lattice clock. On Ye's share, I would draw the line as you did, at the lattice physics, the cavity-stabilised laser and the systematic-control campaign, and not at comb infrastructure, which is the 2005 territory and which I would keep out of the citation on purpose. I am still against waiting for the redefinition. If the decision depends on a committee outside ours, we are in effect awarding the prize for the redefinition and not for the discovery. You and Lindroth share my wish for an expert check of the uncertainty budgets and I support asking for it formally.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B044, magic-angle graphene with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and argues that an unresolved pairing mechanism does not make the discovery early, since the mechanism of the high-Tc cuprates was not settled when they were honoured. He rejects my two-name variant because it drops Bistritzer.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is a fair challenge and I have changed my view on part of it: I now agree that an open mechanism alone is not disqualifying, and that I was too quick to treat it as such. My remaining hesitation is about what the citation can truthfully say. For the cuprates the phenomenon was dramatic and stood for years with a clear before and after, and the credit was settled by the experimental discovery. For B044 the experimental first authors, Cao and Fatemi, are omitted, and the precursor theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) is outside the three names. I also accept your point on Bistritzer: with the 2011 prediction as the theory half of the citation, dropping him weakens the logic, so I withdraw my two-name variant as the main proposal, though I would still support three names if B044 became the leading candidate. I keep B044 as my first alternative and it is where I would go if the committee decides the lattice clock is too close to earlier prizes.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B018 as a quantitatively understood advance, admits the overlap with 2005 and 2012 and the credit of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley, and asks whether my remaining concern is the comb overlap.
responses.response: Yes, the comb overlap was my remaining concern, and your account of the atomic-structure argument has largely removed it: the magic-wavelength condition is a statement about atomic polarisabilities that predates any record uncertainty, so it is a physical idea and not a technical improvement. I would ask that the citation speak of trapping atoms at a magic wavelength, which is the physical content, in addition to the 1e-18 figure. What I cannot judge is how well the many-body and systematic-uncertainty claims stand against the comparisons made since, and for that I rely on your expertise and on a reviewer. Please tell us if there is any way the lattice clock could be seen as a repeat of the Wineland work that I have not considered.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B038, gamma-ray burst afterglows with Costa, Frontera and Kulkarni, as a mature discovery that settled a thirty-year puzzle, concedes the attribution may sink it, and lists B018 and B004 as alternatives.
responses.response: We agree on the science, and the Swift and Fermi confirmation is exactly the independent test I look for. I also appreciate that you would accept an imperfect boundary, but I cannot, and the reason is specific. Costa and Frontera for the BeppoSAX localisation are clear to me. The second part, the optical counterpart and redshift, was shared among van Paradijs, Groot and others, Djorgovski, Metzger and Kulkarni's group, and a single Kulkarni does not represent that step; I also cannot confirm eligibility for some of those people from these files. I would not leave this recognition permanently unawarded, and I would ask the Academy's experts for a report on attribution so it can come back in a later year. I note that you list B018 among your alternatives, so I would ask whether the explanation above, that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct physical idea, is enough for you to support it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee as a whole, and in particular Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson, accepts the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation as a distinct discovery and not a successor to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether Ye's share, as the accuracy, coherence and many-body clock work, satisfies the rule that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a better later realisation.
The current record uncertainties and the inter-laboratory comparisons, which I cannot verify from these files and which expert reviewers should confirm.

Whether I am still discounting B007 and B038 too heavily because my own field makes me sensitive to collaboration-scale credit problems, and whether an expert attribution report could change that for a later year.
statement.conflict_note: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and work in astroparticle physics at KTH. This touches B007 (IceCube neutrino astronomy, my own field) and B038 (gamma-ray burst afterglows, which relates to Fermi-LAT and my gamma-ray polarimetry plans), and I would consider recusing myself from the final decision if either became the leading candidate. As the preferred configuration is B018, which is outside my field, I see no specific conflict, and I know of no connection to Katori or Ye. This is unchanged from round 1.
